title: Grand Lake Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Grand Lake wells have a 130 ft median depth, 8 gpm median yield, and finished costs of about $14,400-$25,000.
h1: What Grand Lake Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Buying land around Grand Lake means looking closely at the well records before you rely on a listing description. The Colorado DWR records include 2,652 permitted wells within five miles of Grand Lake, although only 1,622 are recorded as constructed. Depth and production vary because most permits identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers rather than a consistent shallow water-bearing layer.

The local records point to a typical well that is manageable to drill but not predictable from the surface. The median depth is 130 feet, the median reported yield is 8 gallons per minute, and the median static water level is 60 feet below ground. Those figures are useful for screening a property, not for replacing a site-specific well proposal.

sections.heading: How deep are wells around Grand Lake?
sections.html:
Grand Lake wells have a median reported depth of 130 feet. The middle half runs from 68 to 250 feet, which is the range most useful when asking a driller for an initial bid. It shows that a nearby well may be substantially shallower or deeper than the median without being unusual.

The depth mix adds perspective: 35% are under 100 feet, while 43% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Another 14% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 7% reach 600 feet or more. The deepest recorded well is 1,352 feet. In this mountain setting, fractured granite and gneiss can produce water at very different depths across short distances.

sections.heading: Grand Lake well yield: what can a buyer expect?
sections.html:
Among the 889 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 8.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 5.0 to 11.0 gallons per minute, and 74% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. That is generally a useful production range for a household well, provided the storage and pressure system are properly sized.

Low producers are present but not common in this record set: 1% report under 1 gallon per minute, while 15% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. A yield test matters more than the regional median. Ask for the well construction report, pump information, and any recovery or pumping records before assuming a particular lot will perform like its neighbors.

sections.heading: What the water levels show near Grand Lake
sections.html:
The median static water level is 60 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 25 to 100 feet. Static level means the water depth after the well has recovered, not the depth at which drilling first encountered water. This distinction matters when estimating pump setting, trenching, and pressure-system work.

The decade series does not show a simple continuing decline. Median depth to water was 60 feet in the 1990s, 80 feet in the 2000s, 76 feet in the 2010s, and 60 feet in the 2020s. The records therefore suggest variation rather than a steady drop. Only 169 wells report static water levels, so treat the series as a local reference, not a complete groundwater trend.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Grand Lake, and when?
sections.html:
Permit history is long around Grand Lake. The records show 26 permits from the 1950s, 80 from the 1960s, 356 from the 1970s, 371 from the 1980s, and 618 from the 1990s. There were 521 in the 2000s, 171 in the 2010s, and 188 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most active names in these records are Mcpherson Drilling Company (Mcpherson, Benny Don) with 555 wells, Dale, Genevieve L with 210, and J & J Drilling Inc. (Dale, John U) with 187. These counts describe permit records, not current availability or a recommendation. Confirm licensing, scheduling, scope, and references directly before selecting a contractor.

sections.heading: What does a new well cost at Grand Lake?
sections.html:
Grand Lake drilling is priced around fractured mountain bedrock, commonly granite or gneiss. The cost model uses a drilling rate of $65 to $100 per foot. At the local median depth of 130 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $8,400 to $13,000. That figure is for drilling, not a complete water system.

A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $14,400 to $25,000 at the median depth. A bid can move outside that range when the hole is deeper, access is difficult, casing or grouting requirements change, or the pump and electrical layout is more involved. Get pricing that clearly separates drilling, casing, grout, testing, pump equipment, trenching, and electrical work.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building near Grand Lake
sections.html:
The main water risk is uneven production in fractured bedrock. A neighboring well with an 8.0 gallon-per-minute median yield does not guarantee the same result on your parcel. The records include very deep wells and a small share of low-yield wells, so check surrounding permits for depth, yield, static level, aquifer description, and construction details. A dry hole or disappointing yield is a real possibility that should be addressed in the project budget.

There are 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 historic mine features within about ten miles, with 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That is a reason to test, not proof that a specific well is unsafe. Locate the well away from septic components and other contamination sources, verify setbacks with the applicable authorities, and test existing water before purchase. A DWR permit and an exempt household-use well still require proper construction and use compliance.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Grand Lake, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Grand Lake is 130 feet. The middle half runs from 68 to 250 feet, while 35% are under 100 feet and 43% are between 100 and 300 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss make nearby depths vary, so surrounding well records are more useful than relying on the median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Grand Lake?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65-$100 per foot. At the 130-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $8,400-$13,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is about $14,400-$25,000. Deeper drilling, difficult access, and site-specific construction requirements can change the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do Grand Lake wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 8.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 5.0 to 11.0 gallons per minute. Most reported wells, 74%, produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Low-yield wells are uncommon but present: 1% report under 1 gallon per minute. Require a yield test for the property you are buying.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Grand Lake?
faq.a: The area has 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 historic mine features within about ten miles, but those locations do not determine the quality of an individual well. Test the actual household water before purchase and after construction. Review the well construction record, septic location, and nearby land uses with a qualified water professional.

faq.q: Do Grand Lake wells have enough water for a house?
faq.a: Many reported wells have useful production: the median yield is 8.0 gallons per minute, and 74% produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Still, yield is site-specific in fractured bedrock. Ask for the permit, completion report, pump details, and any pumping test. Confirm the proposed household use is allowed by the DWR permit and applicable rules.
